The verb mill has one central idea running through all its uses: working material through mechanical force to transform it. From that core, it branches into five distinct meanings — from grinding grain to a crowd of confused people.
1. To grind something into powder or small pieces

This is the original, foundational meaning. When you mill grain, coffee beans, pepper, spices, or similar things, you crush and grind them — typically between two hard surfaces — until they become a fine powder or small particles.

  • The wheat was milled into flour at the local mill.
  • She milled fresh coffee beans every morning.
  • He milled the peppercorns into a coarse powder.

The essential idea is reduction: you take something whole and break it down into something finer through grinding. Notice that you can use it with or without into — "mill the grain" or "mill the grain into flour" — both are correct.
2. To cut and shape hard material with a rotating machine

In engineering and manufacturing, to mill something means to cut, shave, or sculpt it using a high-speed rotating cutting tool called a milling machine. The machine spins rapidly and carves away material — usually metal, but also wood or plastic — to produce a very precise shape, surface, or slot.

  • The machinist milled the steel block into a perfectly flat surface.
  • The part was milled to exact specifications.
  • They milled a groove into the aluminum casing.

Think of it as precision sculpting using spinning blades. The result is always something more refined, exact, or shaped than what you started with.
3. To cut fine ridges along the edge of a coin

When coins are manufactured, their edges are often given a ring of tiny, even ridges. The process of cutting those ridges is called milling. When you hear a coin described as having a milled edge, those ridges were mechanically pressed in.

  • The coins were milled along the edges at the mint.
  • A milled edge makes counterfeiting more difficult.

This was done historically to prevent people from scraping metal off the edges of gold or silver coins — any scraping would visibly destroy the ridges. Look at the edge of a quarter or a dime; those ridges are there because the coin was milled.
4. (Of people or animals) To move around slowly, aimlessly, and without direction

This is almost certainly the sense you will encounter most often in modern everyday English, and it has almost no connection to machinery anymore. When a group of people or animals mills around or mills about, they move in a slow, directionless, somewhat restless way — no clear destination, no organized flow, just people wandering and drifting in loose, overlapping paths.

  • Hundreds of people were milling around outside the stadium, waiting for the gates to open.
  • After the ceremony ended, guests milled about the lawn.
  • The cattle milled nervously in the pen.
  • Students milled around in the hallway between classes.

Picture a crowd after a concert ends: nobody is running, nobody is marching, but nobody is standing still either. They're just... drifting, turning, doubling back, moving in no particular direction. That slow, aimless, swirling motion is exactly what mill around captures.

Key things to notice about this sense:

  • It almost always comes with around or about. You rarely say just "they milled" without one of these words.
  • It applies to groups, never to a single person. One person cannot mill around — a crowd can.
  • It carries a slight sense of waiting or uncertainty — people who are milling around are usually waiting for something to happen, or don't know quite what to do next.
  • The movement is not panicked, not purposeful, not still — it's that specific in-between state of slow, uncoordinated group motion.

This sense is absolutely everywhere in fiction, journalism, and everyday speech. A writer describing any crowd scene will very likely reach for this word.
5. (In textiles) To process cloth to make it thicker and denser

In the world of fabric production — especially wool — to mill cloth means to clean and compress the fibers by wetting them and mechanically beating or pressing them together. This makes the fabric denser, tighter, stronger, and more weatherproof.

  • The wool was milled to produce a compact, durable fabric.
  • Milled cloth resists water better than unmilled fabric.

You're most likely to encounter this in historical texts, fashion writing, or descriptions of traditional craftsmanship.
6. (Archaic/British slang) To beat or fight someone

This sense is very old and rarely used today, but you may encounter it in older literature. In past centuries, to mill someone meant to punch or beat them — essentially, to fight.

  • He threatened to mill anyone who stepped in his way.

You can safely ignore this meaning in modern contexts unless you're reading 18th or 19th century British writing.

Here's the through-line that connects nearly all these meanings: mill always involves applying force to material in order to transform or process it. Grain is transformed into flour. Metal is transformed into a precise shape. A coin's edge is transformed into ridges. Cloth is transformed into dense fabric. Even the "milling crowd" sense echoes this — people being "worked" by some invisible force (anticipation, confusion, waiting) that keeps them in motion without letting them settle.

Of all these, the two you will use and encounter most are:

  • "Mill (something)" — to grind it into a powder (coffee, grain, spices).
  • "Mill around/about" — for a crowd moving in slow, aimless, directionless motion.

Master those two and you've captured the word's most living, active uses in modern English.
